item.title: Andros on one page: rebuilding my island map, seven years on
item.dc:creator: Eriola Trungu Impersimi
item.description:
Back in 2019, during my MSc in Geoinformatics, I made a set of maps of Andros. I collected the base data from free online sources, created the digital terrain models myself and designed two printed maps at 1:150,000, one with contours and one with hypsometric tints and hillshading. I also made a web version, served through GeoServer with OpenLayers on top.

It worked well for the course. But it needed a map server running all the time, a styling file for every layer and someone to look after it. That’s not something a small island can realistically keep going.

What was missing

Before starting, I had a look at what’s already out there. The Municipality of Andros publishes its maps as static images. The best interactive maps of the island come from others: Andros Routes, a non-profit, looks after the trail network, and there are hiking maps you can buy. What I couldn’t find was a simple, free map of the whole island that also gives coordinates in the Greek Grid (ΕΓΣΑ87), the system local engineers work with.

The map

The new version is one web page, with no server behind it:

  • Relief first. The 13 m terrain model and the hillshade are blended into one relief image, so you can read the shape of the island straight away.
  • Names that suit the zoom. The generalised 1:150,000 settlements from 2019 decide which village names you see when you zoom out, so that work is still being used.
  • Click anywhere to get the elevation and the coordinates in both WGS84 and ΕΓΣΑ87.
  • Draw a route to get its length, ascent, descent and an elevation profile.
  • Greek and English, with a search that doesn’t mind accents, and its own symbol for every kind of feature.
  • OpenStreetMap layers you can switch on for everyday use: health centres, pharmacies, police and fire stations, municipal offices, fuel, bus stops, springs, viewpoints and the waymarked trails. Each trail opens its own elevation profile.

How I built it

I rebuilt it in Python, coding with Claude: GeoPandas for the vector layers, rasterio for the terrain and Leaflet for the map.

What’s next

I’d like to explore how a map like this could be useful in a council setting, for example for the Municipality of Andros, where a single file can sit inside their existing website with one line of code.

Map: etymo.co.uk/AndrosWebMap

item.title: Do motorcyclists follow variable message signs? What 105 riders in Athens told us
item.dc:creator: Eriola Trungu Impersimi
item.description:
Athens has had variable message signs (VMS), the electronic panels over its main roads, since 2004: 24 of them, run by the city’s traffic management centre, warning drivers about accidents, roadworks and demonstrations ahead. The information they give is designed with car drivers in mind. But a large share of the traffic in Athens is on two wheels: motorcycles and scooters that filter between lanes and rarely sit in the queue the sign is warning about.

So, with Ioanna Spyropoulou at the National Technical University of Athens, I asked: do riders actually change their route when a variable message sign tells them something is wrong ahead?

How we found out

We stopped riders across Athens and asked them to fill in a questionnaire, which wasn’t easy, since many said no. We ended up with 105 complete answers. Each rider saw a set of made-up but realistic VMS messages, varying three things: what the incident was, how bad its impact was, and whether the sign suggested another route. For each one they rated how likely they were to divert. We then used probit models to work out which parts of the message, and which kinds of rider, made a diversion more likely.

What we found

  • Riders like the VMS, but don’t feel they’re for them. Most found them useful, yet 56% didn’t want more money spent on them, and 36% wanted the VMS to show travel times that reflect how two-wheelers actually move.
  • The message matters. The type of incident and how big its impact was both changed whether riders diverted. Roadworks made them most likely to change route.
  • Alternative routes didn’t. Unlike car and professional drivers in earlier studies, riders weren’t swayed by a suggested alternative route. They find their own way.
  • Who the rider is matters too. Riders on bigger motorcycles were more likely to divert, probably because they can’t squeeze through traffic as easily. Habits such as breaking traffic rules, age and gender also played a part.

Why it matters

“Smart city” tools are often designed around one kind of road user. If a city wants its information systems to work for everyone, it has to ask each group what they need. For riders in Athens, that means information that reflects how they move, not how cars queue.

Spyropoulou, I. and Impersimi, E. (2020). Powered-two-wheelers and smart cities: the case of variable message signs. IET Intelligent Transport Systems, 14(14), 2021–2029. doi.org/10.1049/iet-its.2019.0702

item.title: From Athens to London: pedestrian collisions and the built environment, five years on
item.dc:creator: Eriola Trungu Impersimi
item.description:
In 2021 I finished my master’s thesis in Geoinformatics at the National Technical University of Athens. It looked at 1,318 pedestrian collisions in the Municipality of Athens between 2008 and 2017 and asked a simple question: how does the shape of the city relate to where pedestrians are injured?

I found persistent hotspots in the centre, around Omonia, Syggrou and Vasilissis Sofias, and associations with bars and pubs, crossings, traffic signals and bus stops. The thesis ended, as theses do, with a list of things I wished I’d had: time of day, the age of the people involved, socio-economic context, a sense of how busy each place is.

Five years later, I asked the same questions of London. This time I had all of those things.

The data

London is a gift for this kind of work, because almost everything is open:

  • Collisions: the Department for Transport’s STATS19 data. Every police-recorded injury collision, with location, date, time, severity and the age of each casualty.
  • Neighbourhoods: ONS small-area boundaries, the English Indices of Deprivation 2025 and population figures.
  • Streets: OpenStreetMap for crossings, signals, bus stops, stations, schools, pubs and the drivable street network.

From 2021 to 2025 there were 22,108 pedestrian casualties in Greater London. 5,926 of them were killed or seriously injured, and deaths ranged from 36 to 61 a year.

Year Killed Seriously injured Slightly injured Total
2021 36 926 2,878 3,840
2022 42 1,194 3,322 4,558
2023 53 1,223 3,279 4,555
2024 61 1,136 3,254 4,451
2025 51 1,204 3,449 4,704

The low 2021 figure is almost certainly the early-2021 lockdown keeping people off the streets, a reminder that counts always carry the conditions they were collected in.

Lesson one: the denominator changes the story

Ranked by fatal and serious casualties per 100,000 residents, the City of London comes out at 167.6 a year, nearly four times the next borough, Westminster (43.0). Taken at face value, it is by far the most dangerous place to walk in the capital.

It isn’t. Only a few thousand people live in the City, while hundreds of thousands work there or pass through every weekday. Dividing by residents measures something, but not the risk of walking there. Ranked per kilometre of road instead, the order changes substantially.

Lesson two: crossings “correlate” with casualties

Comparing London’s roughly 5,000 small areas, the features that rise most strongly with serious pedestrian casualties per km² were traffic signals and crossings (rank correlations of about +0.4), followed by major roads, bus stops, junctions and pubs and bars. Almost exactly what I found in Athens.

It would be easy, and wrong, to conclude that crossings are dangerous. Two things are going on:

  • Exposure. Crossings, signals, bus stops and pubs are put where lots of people meet lots of traffic. Many of these variables partly measure “how busy is this place”.
  • Reverse causality. Crossings and signals are often installed because a location had collisions. The safety measure follows the problem.

This is why the project goes on to fit a negative binomial model that accounts for how busy each area is, asking which street features still go with more casualties once activity is taken into account. That is the question my thesis couldn’t answer with the data it had.

Finding hotspots along streets, not across them

In Athens I used planar kernel density, the familiar heatmap. Its weakness in a city is that a cluster on one road “leaks” onto a parallel street across a block. For London I measured density along the street network instead: the streets are cut into 50 m pieces and each casualty’s weight spreads along the network for 250 m.

Alongside it, a Getis-Ord Gi* analysis on small areas separates statistically significant clusters from random noise, with a correction for testing thousands of areas at once.

How far is emergency care?

My Athens dashboard showed hospitals next to collisions. In London I went a step further and measured the drive time along the street network from every casualty to the nearest A&E and to the nearest of London’s four major trauma centres, where the most seriously injured are taken.

These are free-flowing times for the hospital journey, not ambulance response times, but they show clearly which parts of London are furthest from trauma care.

Then and now

In 2021 my tools were R and ArcGIS Pro, with Esri Dashboards and StoryMaps for the visuals, and the project took months.

This time I worked with an AI assistant, Claude, and went from research questions to a tested analysis pipeline and a live dashboard in a fraction of the time. The questions, the choice of methods and the judgement about what the results mean came from my research background. The AI made it possible to build and check everything much faster, including testing the model on synthetic data with known answers before trusting it on the real thing.

The whole project uses open data and open-source Python, and anyone can rerun it.

  • Explore the dashboard: etymo.co.uk/london-pedestrian-safety. Try the spotlight on a junction you know, or play the years.
  • Code and methods: github.com/eritrouib/london-pedestrian-safety

What’s next

Two things. First, publishing the Athens work properly, re-analysed with the methods developed here. Second, an AI layer for the London data, so anyone can ask a question in plain English and get an answer computed from the data, with its sources, rather than a guess.

Data: Department for Transport STATS19, ONS, MHCLG (Open Government Licence); OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). Police-recorded data under-reports minor pedestrian injuries, and associations between areas and casualties do not show cause.
